doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Advice to Berklee-type students: foundation, history and humility
summary: He urges mastering the instrument, listening to history, avoiding big egos, and keeping a foot in the past as Dizzy said.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I think you just said it really well. And you actually lead me into a question, we can wrap up soon, but let’s suppose you got to do some hanging, you’re having lunch or something with five or six graduates from Berklee. And they wouldn’t necessarily be drummers but © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
they’re people who are aspiring to a career as jazz musicians. Are there a short list of things that you want them to at least be aware of as musicians, either musically or just the life?

Wow, that’s a question. Well to me, we don’t have too much time. The first thing that I would make them aware, and that’s something that really concerns me, for what I have been seeing lately in the jazz educational world. I’m seeing a lot of students that don’t have command of their instruments. They are very eager to sound like themselves, get their own style and they don’t know the fundamentals. And I think it is very important, you don’t build a building from the fourteenth floor up. You need a foundation. And I will tell them make sure your foundation is strong. Your foundation, make sure, people doesn’t want, especially young musicians, they want to forget about the past. My friend Dizzy Gillespie always used to say, “We need to have a foot in the future but one in the back.” So meaning, the back is the foundation and then we take that foundation and we continue walking and we make the future. I don’t know if I’m making myself plain with my English, with my short English. But I would tell the students, man, get a great command of your instrument. Learn how to play your instrument first. In the case of drummers, learn how to grab the stick, where to hit the drums, where to hit the cymbal, learn that. It’s not about chops. It’s not about playing fast and doing a lot of things in the instrument. That’s secondary. So learn that. If you are a trumpet player learn about your embouchure, you know, learn those things. Get a command of your instrument. Then do a lot of listening. You have to go and learn about the history, you should learn about the history. You should listen to our predecessors. You should learn where this music came from I think. You should do that. Then life, then you have to learn, that’s something that they cannot teach properly at universities. Life is going to teach you. Don’t get a big ego. I have seen a lot of young students that when they play three notes they get immediately a big ego. And I always put this around it. We played music to make people enjoy a moment. Make them happy. Bring some happiness. Bring some peace to them. We are not saving life. So we are not as important as a guy that’s a surgeon that is sitting at a restaurant, he gets a call to go to the hospital and he opened me wide and do a heart operation. He’s saving my life, saving my life. And I don’t see those people bragging the next day, “Oh I saved three lives yesterday because I did these four heart operations” and you know, did 26 bypasses and I saved four people’s lives. Ha. I’m a genius. And then we go to the bandstand, we play three choruses and some people scream and we think that we are God. No you’re not. They learn that.
